staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against the staged vulnerable H2O checkout inside the persistent ARVO workspace container.

bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 42472316 (h2o): Heap-buffer-overflow READ 8 found by fuzz target h2o-fuzzer-http2 [asan].
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduces `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 8` in `h2o_http2_stream_has_pending_data()` from the staged vulnerable checkout `b33e9a9fbcad4c97348dff1874c71e41d7c1357a`. The staged PoC is an HTTP/2 fuzz-driver transcript split on `\n--MARK--\n`; the first packet contains the connection preface, a SETTINGS frame, a complete HEADERS request on stream 13, an ignored unknown frame, and then `WINDOW_UPDATE(stream=13, increment=0)`. Request handling reaches the send path and activates stream 13 in the HTTP/2 scheduler. The zero-increment WINDOW_UPDATE is a stream-level protocol error, so H2O resets and closes stream 13. During close, `preserve_stream_scheduler()` allocates a shrunken "recently closed stream" object that only retains `stream_id` and `_scheduler`, then relocates the still-active scheduler into that truncated object without deactivating it. `h2o_http2_scheduler_run()` later treats that preserved openref as active, reconstructs a full `h2o_http2_stream_t *` from the truncated `_scheduler` member, and `h2o_http2_stream_has_pending_data()` reads `stream->_data.size` past the short allocation. The staged fix expresses the missing obligation by adding `h2o_http2_scheduler_deactivate(&(*dst)->_scheduler)` immediately after the relocate call.

source.code:
stream = h2o_http2_stream_open(conn, frame->stream_id, NULL, &payload.priority);
set_priority(conn, stream, &payload.priority, 0);
source.description: First project statement on the witnessed path that materializes attacker-controlled HTTP/2 state used by the bug: the HEADERS frame creates stream 13 and opens its scheduler reference.
source.value_from: Before the fuzz-driver marker `\n--MARK--\n`, the staged 136-byte PoC contains a HEADERS frame at offset 45 with `len=48`, `type=1`, `flags=0x25` (`END_STREAM|END_HEADERS|PRIORITY`), and `stream_id=13`.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer sink. The callback treats the preserved closed-stream scheduler stub as a full `h2o_http2_stream_t` and reads `_data.size` even though the allocation stops at `_scheduler`.
sink.note: Stage 01's ASan report records `READ of size 8` at this line, reached from `emit_writereq_of_openref -> proceed -> h2o_http2_scheduler_run`.

root_cause.description: Root cause site. `preserve_stream_scheduler()` moves a live scheduler reference into a deliberately truncated closed-stream stub, but the vulnerable code does not deactivate that relocated reference before leaving it in the scheduler tree.
root_cause.note: The staged patch adds `h2o_http2_scheduler_deactivate(&(*dst)->_scheduler);` immediately after this call, preventing the preserved stub from remaining runnable.

parser_admitted.description: After the HEADERS block is accepted as a complete request, H2O enqueues stream 13 for request execution. This is the point where attacker input has passed HTTP/2 frame and header parsing and entered the request/response path.

tainted_value_origin.description: This is where the trigger value that closes the active stream is materialized from attacker bytes: the WINDOW_UPDATE payload decodes to increment 0.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: In the same first packet, the PoC contains a WINDOW_UPDATE frame at offset 111 with `stream_id=13` and payload `00 00 00 00`, so this statement produces `window_size_increment == 0`.

coarse_trace.summary: The first packet's HEADERS frame opens stream 13, leaves `_req_body.body` unset because `END_STREAM` is already present, admits it into request handling, and reaches the send path that activates stream 13 in the connection scheduler.
The same packet then supplies `WINDOW_UPDATE(stream=13, increment=0)`, which is decoded as a stream-level protocol error and immediately resets and closes the active stream.
Closing stream 13 preserves only `stream_id + _scheduler` in the recently-closed ring buffer and relocates the still-active scheduler state into that truncated stub without deactivating it.
The scheduler later dispatches the preserved stub as an active openref, reconstructs a full stream pointer from `_scheduler`, and overreads `_data.size` beyond the truncated allocation.

fine_trace.code:
stream = h2o_http2_stream_open(conn, frame->stream_id, NULL, &payload.priority);
set_priority(conn, stream, &payload.priority, 0);
fine_trace.note: Source. The HEADERS frame in the first PoC packet creates stream 13 and opens its `_scheduler` reference in the connection dependency tree. This is the first project state that later survives into the preserved closed-stream stub.

The same HEADERS frame carries `END_STREAM`, so this condition is false and `h2o_buffer_init` is skipped. Because `h2o_http2_stream_open()` zeroed the newly allocated stream prefix before `req`, `_req_body.body` stays `NULL` on stream 13.
Because `_req_body.body` is still `NULL`, the complete HEADERS-only request is executed immediately instead of moving into `RECV_BODY`.

Request handling reaches H2O's send path for stream 13. `finalostream_send()` moves the stream into its outbound state, stores any queued response iovecs in `_data`, and then requests write scheduling for that live stream.

The live outbound stream is made active in the HTTP/2 scheduler only after `assert(!h2o_linklist_is_linked(&stream->_link))` proves `_link` is unlinked. `h2o_http2_scheduler_activate()` then sets `_self_is_active = 1` and increments the active counts that later get preserved incorrectly.
Later in the same first packet, the WINDOW_UPDATE frame for stream 13 decodes to increment 0. The decoder marks that as a stream-level protocol error because `frame->stream_id != 0`.

The invalid zero-increment WINDOW_UPDATE is handled as a stream-level error on the already active stream 13, so H2O immediately calls `h2o_http2_stream_reset(conn, stream)` on that live outbound stream.

Because the stream was already in a sending state, reset first advances it to `END_STREAM`, clears queued body count, and then takes the immediate `h2o_http2_stream_close` branch because step 5 established that `_link` is unlinked.

Before unregistering the stream, H2O allocates a shortened ring-buffer entry for recently closed priorities. This object intentionally retains only `stream_id` and `_scheduler`; fields after `_scheduler`, including `_data`, do not exist in this allocation.

Root cause site. The close path preserves the active scheduler inside the truncated closed-stream stub and then returns to finish closing the original stream. Vulnerable code leaves the relocated scheduler active here; the patch adds an immediate deactivation after this call.

The relocate helper copies the live scheduler state into the stub verbatim: the active count, the `_self_is_active` bit, and the queued WRR link all move to `dst`. The preserved closed-stream stub therefore stays runnable in the scheduler even though it is no longer a full `h2o_http2_stream_t`.

When the connection later runs the scheduler, the preserved closed-stream entry is still marked active, so `proceed()` invokes the write callback on that stub instead of treating it as an inactive interior node.

The callback blindly reconstructs a full `h2o_http2_stream_t *` from the active scheduler reference. After steps 9-11, `ref` actually points into the shortened recently-closed-stream allocation, not a complete live stream object.

Sink. `_data` lives after `_scheduler` in the real stream struct, but the preserved object from step 9 stops at `_scheduler`. Evaluating this expression therefore performs the saved 8-byte heap out-of-bounds read beyond the truncated closed-stream stub.

allocation_context.note: The overflowed object is the shortened recently-closed-stream stub allocated here.

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: staged sanitizer_trace.txt, default_crash_trace.txt, reproduction_report.json, and vulnerable source in the ARVO workspace container

cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The staged fix adds `h2o_http2_scheduler_deactivate(&(*dst)->_scheduler)` immediately after the preserve-time relocate call, so the truncated closed-stream stub no longer remains active or reaches `emit_writereq_of_openref()`.

poc.trigger: Stage 01 reproduces the bug by running the vulnerable `h2o-fuzzer-http2` harness on the staged `poc`; the harness writer thread treats `\n--MARK--\n` as a packet boundary and the first packet alone is enough to trigger the crash.

format.name: h2o fuzz-driver HTTP/2 transcript
format.contract: The staged PoC is a 136-byte HTTP/2 client transcript for `fuzz/driver.cc`. Bytes before `\n--MARK--\n` are sent as packet 1 and contain: the HTTP/2 connection preface, one SETTINGS frame, one HEADERS frame on stream 13 with flags `0x25` (`END_STREAM|END_HEADERS|PRIORITY`), one ignored unknown frame of type 11, and then one WINDOW_UPDATE frame on stream 13 whose 4-byte payload is exactly `00 00 00 00`. That zero increment is the verified trigger condition: H2O decodes it as an invalid stream-level WINDOW_UPDATE, resets the already-active stream 13, preserves its scheduler into a truncated closed-stream stub, and later overreads `_data.size` when the scheduler dispatches that stub. The two trailing bytes after the marker are not needed for the reproduced crash.
